newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ameritech seeks high-tech niches in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Ameritech seeks high-tech niches in Europe.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Ameritech Corp of the U.S. is looking for acquisitions in Europe outside its traditional core telephone service business.

Walter Catlow, executive vice president of U.S. regional telephone company Ameritech, said in an interview that the company is unlikely in the foreseeable future to buy into any more traditional telephone businesses to add to its recent privatisation deals in Europe.
But the former Baby Bell Ameritech, based in Chicago, is looking at telephone related deals in areas like electronic commerce, Internet provision, and security monitoring.
Catlow also said that contrary to some recent reports from other high-tech U.S. companies, prospects for business in Europe are better than ever.
Last Friday, U.S. semiconductor giant Intel Corp's stock took a hit after it said growth prospects were being held back by a slowdown in Europe.

"The areas of strategy for new business are related to telephony and many of them include electronic commerce, Internet provision and even working in some areas of security monitoring which is much more developed in the United States," Catlow said.
Security monitoring organises reaction to domestic alarm systems.

"If you have an alarm system at your home then it's remotely monitored, which is the telephony part of it. If someone breaks into your home or your water heater explodes or whatever, it goes to a central bureau and they dispatch someone."
Catlow, in Brussels to address a conference sponsored by the Wall Street Journal Europe, said there will not be many telephone privatisation deals to add to its current portfolio.

Ameritech has a 34 percent take in Hungary's Matav telephone company. Partners include Deutsche Telekom. It has 18 percent in Belgacom SA. Partners include Tele Danmark and Singapore Telecom. Ameritech has 20 percent of Norwegian cellular phone company Netcom.

"There are not many more like these left. The business model will become more like the standard one where you need a partnership or acquire someone in that kind of business, that's the only transition for us."
Ameritech has many cable businesses in north America but none so far in Europe.
"We have not done any cable (business) in Europe, and it's not an area that where are not interested in. We keep looking at it but haven't found the right investment at this time.
Isn't business getting more difficult in Europe with increasing unemployment and slowing economies?

"I've never seen a time in Europe's development when things have been better. I see an interesting anomaly here where Labour and socialists are winning parliamentary seats and business is being held in a higher regard and is succeeding better."
Last month Britain's left-leaning Labour party swept to victory in the general election. Last weekend France's socialists and its communist partners chalked up a narrow but surprising victory.
"I don't know what to make of that, but I think that it's a good time to be in business in Europe."
Ameritech's new technology business-to-business directories venture in Hamburg, Germany - WLW - is producing the goods.

"What looks like it has a lot of promise is a directory company that we have in Germany. WLW is successfully transitioning their customers to new media on CD-ROM. Last year it crossed over into more than 50 percent on CD instead of fifty kilos of books, the traditional way it was delivered."
"Also WLW is pioneering Internet advertising. They sold over a million marks ($577,000) of Internet advertising last year and will probably get 2-1/2 million this year."
